content: A small ear stimulation device could offer a new way to tackle high blood pressure that stays elevated despite medication. Researchers at Queen Mary University of London have tested a device that stimulates nerves through the ear in people whose high blood pressure remained uncontrolled despite medication. The trial, published in the American Heart Association journal Hypertension , found that the treatment was safe and practical to use at home. Finding additional ways to control blood pressure matters because many people receiving treatment still exceed recommended targets. Persistently high blood pressure increases the risk of cardiovascular disease, including heart attack and stroke. The approach, transcutaneous autonomic neuromodulation (tAN), delivers electrical stimulation without an invasive procedure. It targets the autonomic nervous system, which helps regulate blood pressure through functions outside conscious control. The handheld device, developed by Afferent Medical Solutions, delivers gentle electrical pulses through two clips attached to the tragus, the small piece of cartilage at the front of the ear. Patients can administer the treatment themselves at home. The NIHR-funded SCRATCH-HTN trial included 63 participants whose hypertension remained uncontrolled while taking one or more blood pressure medications. They were randomly assigned to receive either active stimulation or a sham device, allowing researchers to compare outcomes between the groups. Participants used their devices for 30 minutes daily during the first two weeks, then once weekly for another 10 weeks. They followed the schedule closely, and treatment was safe and well tolerated during the trial. Those findings establish that the approach was practical to use but do not establish that it effectively lowers blood pressure compared to sham devices. Across the full study population, active treatment did not produce a significantly greater blood pressure reduction than the sham device. However, a subgroup analysis planned before the trial found a larger reduction with active treatment among people who began with more severe hypertension. That result provides a direction for further research. Larger trials focused on specific patient groups will need to establish whether the difference holds up and identify who, if anyone, benefits. Dr. Ajay Gupta, the chief investigator, a clinical reader at Queen Mary University of London and a consultant physician at Barts Health NHS Trust, said: “This is an exciting, highly patient-acceptable technology that could ultimately provide a cheap, scalable solution for millions. Although the trial did not achieve significance across the broad unselected group, those with more severe hypertension exhibited a clear blood pressure reduction in the active group compared to sham. “As the first and most thorough study of its kind, this points towards important new research directions that could help us understand whether non-invasive neuromodulation can benefit particular groups of patients with uncontrolled hypertension.” Reference: “Safety, Acceptability and Efficacy of Noninvasive Transcutaneous-Autonomic Neuromodulation in Uncontrolled Hypertension” by Ajay Gupta, David Collier, James Steckelmacher, Jane Field, George Collett, Olivier Zongo, Mital Patel, Manish Saxena, Annastazia Learoyd, Amrita Ahluwalia and Peter Sever, 28 September 2026, Hypertension . title: Roller coaster death and injuries leave fans asking whether the thrill is worth the risk
content: The death of a 42-year-old man on a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia this week has raised important questions about amusement park safety. The tragic incident follows reports of serious injuries on other roller coasters, including riders who required emergency brain surgery . Roller coasters are designed to deliver thrills through sudden drops, sharp turns and rapid changes in speed, but what kinds of injuries can these forces cause? How common are these injuries. Are some people more vulnerable than others? And is the thrill worth the risk? With Six Flags Over Georgia set to reopen Friday, I spoke with CNN wellness expert Dr. Leana Wen to help us understand the potential health risks of roller coasters and what riders should know before getting on one. Wen is an emergency physician and clinical associate professor at George Washington University. She previously served as Baltimore’s health commissioner. CNN: How safe are roller coasters? What types of serious injuries are the most common? Dr. Leana Wen: Serious injuries on roller coasters are uncommon when taking into account the enormous number of rides taken every year. According to the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions, the chance of sustaining a serious injury on a ride at a fixed-site US amusement park is approximately one in 15.5 million rides. This statistic is limited because it includes all amusement park rides, not only roller coasters. Also, not every injury is necessarily reported. Moreover, people should be aware that this data comes from an industry-sponsored entity. There is no independent national database capturing every amusement park injury and death. As for types of serious injuries, most are related to the fact that roller coasters expose riders to substantial physical forces. These include gravitational forces, commonly known as G-forces, that increase or decrease the pressure riders feel on their bodies during rapid acceleration and deceleration. Severe injuries can occur because of the forces experienced during a ride, collisions, problems with restraints or other mechanical and operational incidents. It is necessary to distinguish the cause of an injury from the circumstances in which it occurred. The investigation into the death at Six Flags Over Georgia is ongoing and we currently don’t know if the cause of that tragedy is the same as the mechanism behind the brain injuries reported on another Six Flags roller coaster. CNN: How can someone sustain a serious brain injury on a roller coaster without hitting their head? Wen: A direct blow to the head can cause traumatic brain injury, but so can rapid acceleration, deceleration, and changes in direction that lead to the head moving abruptly. The brain is suspended in fluid inside the skull, and sudden movement can cause the brain to shift relative to the surrounding structures. One possible injury is a subdural hematoma , which is bleeding between the brain and its outer protective covering putting pressure on the brain. This very serious injury was what was sustained by several riders after riding the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California, including two who required emergency brain surgery . Other possible injuries include concussions and damage to brain tissue caused by rapid movement within the skull. Sudden forces can also cause bleeding in other areas around or within the brain. In some cases, symptoms can resolve with time; in others, there may be permanent neurological damage or death. CNN: What other kinds of injuries can roller coasters cause? Wen: Roller coasters’ jerking movements can strain the muscles and ligaments supporting the neck, producing symptoms similar to whiplash after a car accident that include neck pain, stiffness and headaches. Some symptoms appear immediately, while others develop over the evening and the following day. Most uncomplicated muscle strains improve with symptomatic treatment, but some could develop neurological complications. Even more common but less serious, roller coasters can provoke dizziness, nausea and motion sickness. These symptoms occur because the brain receives conflicting information from the eyes and the balance organs in the inner ear. They usually resolve not long after the ride ends. A much rarer but extremely serious potential consequence is cervical artery dissection . This occurs when a tear develops in the inner lining of an artery supplying blood to the brain. Sudden neck movements can contribute to this injury, and there have been case reports of dissections following roller coaster rides. This is a potentially life-threatening condition that can cause a stroke. CNN: Are certain people at higher risk of injury from roller coasters? Wen: Yes. People with certain medical conditions should be particularly cautious about intense, high-speed rides. Those with significant neck or back problems, spinal instability or recent orthopedic injuries may be more vulnerable to worsening pain or additional injury. Someone recovering from surgery should check with their surgeon before participating in roller coaster rides. People with cardiovascular conditions also need to consider the physical and emotional stress of the ride and whether the excitement and sudden changes in motion can increase heart rate and blood pressure. Individuals with unstable heart disease, serious arrhythmias or poorly controlled high blood pressure should avoid rides that warn against these conditions. Similarly, people who have known brain aneurysms, prior strokes or serious neurological conditions should consult their physicians before going on these rides. People taking blood-thinning medications also need to take additional caution because there is increased risk of bleeding should they experience an injury. There are other special categories of more vulnerable people, including pregnant women, who should avoid high-intensity roller coasters because of the abrupt movements and acceleration forces. Families with children should also check carefully that the kids meet the ride’s height and restraint requirements, which are designed to ensure that the safety equipment fits correctly. CNN: What symptoms after riding a roller coaster should prompt medical attention? Wen: Anyone who develops a sudden, severe headache, especially one unlike any headache they have experienced before, should seek emergency medical care. The same applies to a headache accompanied by repeated vomiting, confusion, unusual sleepiness or changes in vision. Stroke symptoms also require immediate attention. These include sudden weakness or numbness, particularly on one side of the body, difficulty speaking, facial drooping, loss of balance or trouble walking. Severe or unusual neck pain, particularly when accompanied by a headache, dizziness or neurological symptoms, could indicate cervical artery dissection. Head to the nearest hospital. You can also let the staff at the amusement park know; they can assist you in locating the nearest emergency room or in calling 911. Those symptoms need emergent evaluation. Keep in mind that symptoms can emerge after you’ve finished the rides and left the amusement park. A person who develops a persistent or worsening headache or neck pain hours after a ride should not assume that it’s motion sickness or a neck strain. They need to get urgent medical attention. CNN: What precautions should people take to reduce their risk of injury? Wen: In general, people who have underlying medical issues should receive medical clearance from their clinicians so that they know what type of rides they may want to avoid at the amusement park. Before boarding, read the ride’s posted safety requirements and health warnings. Do not ride if you do not meet the height or other physical requirements, or if you have a medical condition specifically listed as a reason to avoid the attraction. CNN: Given these incidents, should most people stop riding roller coasters? Wen: I think people should take into account the fact is that millions of people enjoy amusement parks every year without sustaining injuries. The available statistics indicate that severe injuries are rare. At the same time, people should recognize that roller coasters, especially the ones involving high speeds and lots of sudden turns and twists, are not risk-free. There are many ways to enjoy amusement parks without going on the fastest or most intense rides. Families can choose attractions based on their preferences and comfort levels.

Vanillin could help form wound-care materials while supplying antibacterial activity, a combination made more practical by its low-cost and abundant supply. The compound behind vanilla’s sweet aroma could become an ingredient in wound-care materials. A team from Flinders University’s Biomedical Nanoengineering Laboratory has found that vanillin has pronounced antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial properties, making it a candidate for formulations designed to help wounds heal. The researchers examined vanillin through a food-to-function framework, connecting its chemistry with its biological activity and potential biomedical uses. Those possibilities include incorporating it into materials and using it to help deliver drugs. Professor Krasimir Vasilev, Professor of Biomedical Nanotechnology at Flinders University and Director of Flinders’ Biomedical Nanoengineering Laboratory, says, “Because vanillin’s synthetic form is abundant and cost-effective, we believe vanillin-based formulations may offer safe and multifunctional solutions for ulcer treatment and targeted drug delivery, especially of hydrophobic compounds. “Owing to its amphiphilic molecular structure, vanillin can interact with reactive oxygen species, cellular membranes, and polymeric matrices, providing a basis for its incorporation into functional formulations.” Amphiphilic molecules contain both water-attracting and water-repelling regions, while hydrophobic compounds do not dissolve readily in water. In material design, vanillin can also serve as a dynamic crosslinker, helping form reversible connections between the long molecular chains that make up polymers. It can therefore contribute to a material’s structure as well as its biological activity. Vanillin is the primary chemical component extracted from natural vanilla pods, but it can also be produced synthetically from clove oil or rice. Its widespread use in foods gives researchers a familiar starting point for exploring other applications. “Vanillin is among the most widely used flavor compounds in the global food system, valued for its sensory attributes, chemical stability, and long history of safety—and that can be transferred to other areas, such as medical uses,” says Vasilev. The researchers see practical advantages in vanillin’s availability as a low-cost small molecule suitable for good manufacturing practices. These characteristics could support industrial-scale production, consistent formulations, and reliable supply chains. The laboratory’s interest in food-derived medical materials grew partly from Vasilev’s experience of eating peppermint leaves from a drink and noticing significant relief from a sore throat. That observation prompted him to investigate whether peppermint’s biological activity could be incorporated into a durable coating through plasma technology, a field he has researched for more than two decades. In work published in the journal Small in February 2026, the Flinders team created a nanoscale coating derived from peppermint oil. The coating protects against infection, inflammation, and oxidative stress while remaining compatible with human tissue and suitable for use on medical materials. The vanillin research continues this exploration of food compounds as potential ingredients in medical technologies. “With coordinated engagement between academia, clinicians, and industry, vanillin has the potential to progress from an underutilized bioactive to a clinically deployable component of next-generation wound care and regenerative therapeutics,” says Vasilev. Reference: “Vanillin as a bioactive component in biomedical formulations for chronic wound healing and tissue regeneration” by Borislav Stoilov, Vi Khanh Truong, Christopher Delaney and Krasimir Vasilev, 2 August 2026, International Journal of Pharmaceutics .
